response.title: How do I run the hot air hose from a portable air conditioner out of a tent without melting the mesh or letting heat back in?
response.answer:
The best solution is to run the portable AC exhaust hose through a rigid, insulated pass-through panel, rather than directly through the tent mesh. This protects the mesh from heat, minimizes hot-air leakage, and keeps insects out.

Recommended setup
Shop
Example of a rigid exhaust pass-through panel. The same principle works with a tent door or mesh opening.
1. Make an insulated exhaust panel

Use a piece of rigid foam insulation board, approximately ½–1 inch thick, or a thin rigid plastic panel with insulation attached.

Cut the panel to fit a portion of the tent's door or window opening.

Cut a circular hole matching your AC exhaust hose diameter, typically 5 or 6 inches.

Install a plastic or metal duct flange in the hole.

Connect the AC hose to the flange using the manufacturer's adapter.

Seal around the flange with foil HVAC tape.

A rigid flange keeps the hot exhaust hose from resting against the mesh.

2. Protect the mesh and tent fabric
Conceptual cross-section: the panel separates the hot duct from the mesh, with the exhaust directed outdoors.

Ideally, use a tent door opening rather than cutting the mesh. Close the zipper around the panel as much as possible.

If the hose must pass near mesh or polyester fabric:

Maintain an air gap between the hose and fabric.

Use a rigid sleeve or flange to prevent contact.

Don't rely on foil tape stuck directly to mesh as thermal protection.

Check the AC manufacturer's required clearances and maximum hose length.

3. Prevent hot air from coming back inside

The most important detail is sealing the opening around the panel.

Use adhesive-backed foam weatherstripping around the panel edges and a removable fabric flap or hook-and-loop strips to close remaining gaps. Avoid ordinary duct tape, which can lose adhesion in heat.

Keep the exhaust outlet outside the tent and pointed away from openings. Don't position it underneath the rainfly or in an enclosed vestibule, where heat can accumulate.

One important consideration: single-hose vs. dual-hose AC

Type

	

What happens in a tent




Single-hose portable AC

	

Exhausts indoor air, drawing replacement warm outdoor air through gaps




Dual-hose portable AC

	

Uses outdoor air for condenser cooling, reducing unwanted warm-air infiltration

A dual-hose portable AC is usually much more efficient for a tent, especially if you can seal both hose openings.

A single-hose AC can still work, but even a perfectly sealed exhaust panel won't eliminate the warm air being pulled back into the tent elsewhere.

My suggested approach

For a typical camping tent, I'd use a removable insulated panel mounted in the lower part of the zippered door, with a rigid duct flange and foam weatherstripping. It avoids permanently modifying the mesh and is easy to remove when packing up.

Also, keep the AC unit level, manage condensate, and use an outdoor-rated power connection with GFCI protection. Don't operate the unit where rain or condensation can reach electrical components.

Two questions: Is your tent a regular polyester camping tent with mesh windows, or a canvas/glamping tent? And is your portable AC a single-hose or dual-hose model?

Those details will determine the cleanest way to mount the exhaust without damaging the tent.
